questions.enonce_markdown:
Abraham has been referred to as "the trust worthy servant of the Lord Most High." Do you agree?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Abraham (called Abram at first) is presented in Genesis 11-25 as the father of the Hebrew people and the first of the patriarchs. To be called a "trustworthy servant" of God means that he was faithful, obedient and reliable in his relationship with God. The Genesis narrative shows that he largely deserves the description, but it does not hide his weaknesses. The answer is therefore a qualified "yes".

**1. Evidence that Abraham was a trustworthy servant.**
(i) *Obedience to the call.* In Genesis 12 God told Abraham to leave his country, his kindred and his father's house for a land that God would show him. Abraham went, without knowing the destination, leaving security for a promise.
(ii) *Faith in God's promises.* Genesis 15 states that Abraham believed the Lord and that God reckoned it to him as righteousness. He trusted the promise of descendants and land although he and Sarah were old and childless.
(iii) *Acceptance of the covenant.* In Genesis 17 Abraham accepted the covenant and its sign, circumcision, for himself and for every male of his household. In doing so he committed his whole household to God.
(iv) *Readiness to offer Isaac.* In Genesis 22 God tested Abraham by asking for his son Isaac, the child of the promise. Abraham prepared to obey and was stopped at the last moment by the angel of the Lord. Many readers consider this the supreme proof of his trust in God.
(v) *Intercession and hospitality.* In Genesis 18 Abraham welcomed the three visitors generously and then pleaded with God for the righteous in Sodom, showing concern for others and a close relationship with God. He also worshipped God by building altars wherever he settled (Shechem, Bethel, Hebron).
(vi) *Integrity and peace-making.* He gave Lot the choice of land to avoid a quarrel (Genesis 13) and rescued him when he was captured (Genesis 14). In the same chapter he paid a tenth to Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, and refused to enrich himself from the spoils. The title "Most High" appears in this episode.

**2. Evidence that points the other way.**
(i) In Egypt (Genesis 12) and again before Abimelech of Gerar (Genesis 20) Abraham passed Sarah off as his sister out of fear for his own safety, putting her and the promise at risk.
(ii) In Genesis 16 Abraham and Sarah, tired of waiting, produced an heir through Hagar, which brought rivalry and family conflict. Genesis 17 also records that Abraham fell down laughing at the promise of a son by Sarah.
(iii) His journey down to Egypt during the famine (Genesis 12) can also be read as a lapse of trust that God would provide.

**3. Assessment.** These failures are real, but they are occasional, and the narrator does not conceal them. They show Abraham as a human believer, not a perfect one. Each time God renews the promise and Abraham returns to obedience. The overall direction of his life, from Ur and Haran to Moriah, is one of trust. Later biblical tradition looks back on him as the model of faith and as "the friend of God", a description found in later books such as Isaiah and 2 Chronicles.

**Conclusion.** I agree, with qualification. Abraham was a trustworthy servant of the Lord Most High because he obeyed the call, believed the promise, accepted the covenant and was ready to give up Isaac. His moral slips in Egypt and Gerar and his impatience over the promise show that his trust was tested and sometimes failed, but they do not cancel the verdict of the tradition that he is the father of those who believe.
